title: ⭐ Practice: apostrophes, road words and a rising fear

questions.prompt: Three girls share one room. Complete: "The ___ room is on the first floor."
questions.explanation: "girls'" is right: the owners are several and their plural already ends in s, so the apostrophe is simply added after that s. "girl's" would give the room to one girl only. "girls" carries no apostrophe at all and says nothing about owning, and "girls's" adds a second s to a plural that has one already.

questions.prompt: On the empty road the other car came up level with her, passed her and went in front. Which verb of the lesson says that?
questions.explanation: "to overtake" is the verb: it names exactly the move of passing another car and taking the place in front of it. "to brake" is the opposite move, slowing down. "to grip" is to hold something very tightly, which is what her hands do on the wheel, and "to gather" is to pick things up, the verb of the first line of the story.

questions.prompt: A driver writes: "My hands were gripping the steering wheel and my heart was thumping." What do those two verbs tell you about her?
questions.explanation: "She was frightened." is right: gripping means holding very tightly and a thumping heart beats hard and fast, and those two together are the body of somebody in fear. "She was quite relieved." would come after the fear has gone, and a relieved body loosens instead of gripping. "She was very surprised." would need something sudden, and "She was uncomfortable." is far too weak for a heart that thumps.

questions.prompt: Your friend looks tired at the end of the afternoon and you want to offer him an idea. Which sentence makes a suggestion?

options.text: What if the boss stops paying the workers?
What this child needs is a good education.
What about another cup of tea?

questions.explanation: "What about another cup of tea?" is the suggestion: the frame What about, followed by a noun or an -ing verb, offers an idea instead of asking for a fact. "What do you mean exactly?" asks for a clarification. "What this child needs is a good education." insists on one point, and "What if the boss stops paying the workers?" expresses a fear about something that has not happened.

questions.prompt: The books belong to the children of the family. Complete: "the ___ books are on the bottom shelf."
questions.explanation: "children's" is right: children is already a plural, but it does not end in s, so it takes the ordinary apostrophe and s of a single owner. "childrens'" and "childrens" both invent a plural in s that English does not have for this word, and "children'" uses the form reserved for plurals that already end in s.

questions.prompt: Judge this statement about the story: "She was travelling by daytime." Which answer gives the right judgement and a justification?

options.text: True: she could see the other car clearly in her mirror.
True: she left the centre a long while before the sun went down.
False: her watch showed half past ten and she said goodnight.
False: the road was busy with cars taking people home from work.

questions.explanation: "False: her watch showed half past ten and she said goodnight." is the answer: the judgement is wrong and the proof comes from the text itself, which is what a justification means. "True: she left the centre a long while before the sun went down." invents a detail nobody wrote. "False: the road was busy with cars taking people home from work." reaches the right judgement with a false proof, and a false proof loses the mark; "True: she could see the other car clearly in her mirror." mistakes headlights in the dark for daylight.
